job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Zane Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Everyone I talk to is made up for this study, so there are no right answers. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I get up at seven and catch the 7.40 bus into Derby. I'm a junior tester at a firm that makes software for delivery companies. I click through new versions of the app, write down what breaks, and send the list to the developers. It's steady, a bit dull, and I like that. After work I cook, go to the climbing wall, or fix my mate's laptop in our shared house.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you land the job, and what was your degree?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I did computer science at Nottingham and finished with a 2:1. I did one eight-week placement at a council IT office, mostly checking forms for bugs. The testing job came through my lecturer's old classmate, and I started in June. I'm on a graduate contract at typical pay, I owe about eleven thousand in student loan and I have two months of rent put away. My dad drives a bus and says he'd help if I got stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected. Every few years something is going to change everything, and then it makes the spell checker a bit better. At work I'd shrug. My housemates would probably laugh, because I still write my test notes in a plain text file.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm relieved, but not calm. My job is clicking through screens and writing down faults, and a little automation already does some of that. I just want the next five years to look like the last five, with one slow raise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as now. I'd keep my two months of rent in the savings account and try to stretch it to three by Christmas. I'd stay in the shared house on Osmaston Road, because the rent is about half what a flat alone would cost. I still wouldn't touch the AI tools they keep pushing at us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly steady, but with a low hum of worry. The loan, the rent and the contract all sit on one small pay cheque. If the firm lost a big customer, junior testers would be first out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen to you if the firm lost its biggest customer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The firm has about forty people, and Parcelworks is a third of the income. If Parcelworks left, I think they'd stop hiring and then let the newest people go, which is me and one other graduate. I'd go back to my parents' spare room in Long Eaton for a while. My dad wouldn't make a fuss, but I'd feel I'd gone backwards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say you never use AI tools. Is that a choice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's partly stubbornness. My manager showed me a tool that writes test cases and I just said I'd rather learn it by doing it by hand. I know that's a risk, but I don't trust something I can't explain, and I'd like my job to be about people who know what they're doing.

say: It's mostly **hype**, and I'll keep doing my job the same way.
I'd tell friends the tools save a little time and no more.
think: I'm **relieved**, but my job is routine testing and a bit of automation could still reach it.
My real worry is the **debt** and one small pay cheque, not AI itself.
do: Keep the **same routine** and stay in the shared house.
Stretch my savings from two months of rent to **three months** by Christmas.
feel: Steady on the surface, with a **low hum** of worry about the loan.
S0.quote: I just want the next five years to look like the last five, with one slow raise.
fieldNote: Wants **stability** above everything; the plain-text notes habit shows how much he prefers the familiar.
Not afraid of AI itself but of a thin pay cheque and a single big customer.
Says he never uses AI tools; partly stubbornness, which he admits.

steps.text: Keep testing delivery app releases the same way
Save one extra month of rent by Christmas

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say the testers need protecting. If software starts writing and checking the test cases, someone has to decide who still has a job. I'd bring it up with the union rep, and online I'd probably post that new tools should come with a deal for the people they replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job is exactly what gets taken first. Checking and finding faults is the kind of work they said would go to AI. I have one year of experience and I'm the cheap junior, so I could be cut or never get promoted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finally join the union branch, because my dad has pushed me for years. I'd ask my manager to put me on the part of the product that talks to real drivers, where someone has to explain things. I'd also start trying the AI test tool, slowly, in my own time, so I'm not the one who refused.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It makes me tense. I don't hate the technology, but I hate being the one with no say. I'd feel like I was waiting for a letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the union actually do for a junior tester?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, maybe not much in the first year. But if the firm tried to cut four testers quietly, a union could demand notice, a say and some retraining money. A group has more weight than one worried graduate on a short contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill goes first if your pay stopped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not the rent, since it's my housemates too. I'd stop the climbing wall and my phone upgrade, and I'd start paying less than the loan minimum, which I hate. After that I'd borrow from my dad, and he'd say yes with a sigh.

say: Workers need a **say**, and new tools should come with a deal for people replaced.
I'd raise it with the **union rep** at work.
think: Checking for faults is the **first thing** AI takes, and I'm the cheap junior.
I could be cut or **never promoted**.
do: Join the **union branch** my dad keeps pushing.
Ask my manager for a role talking to **real drivers**.
Try the AI test tool slowly in my own time.
feel: **Tense**, like waiting for a letter, because I have no say.
S1.quote: A group has more weight than one worried graduate on a short contract.
fieldNote: First sign of his progressive politics turning into practical action: the **union**.
Reluctant AI use only as self-protection, not interest.
Knows his own exposure clearly: a junior tester is the cheapest cut.

steps.text: Join the union branch at the firm this winter
Ask to move onto the driver support side
Try the AI test-case tool for an hour a week
Pause the climbing wall membership and phone upgrade

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is bigger than any one firm, and governments have to act now. Two years is nothing. At work I'd go quiet, to be honest, because nobody in my office has a plan, and online I'd back anything that slows it down and puts support in place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my career could be over before it starts. A computer science degree was meant to be the safe choice. If AI can do all desk work by 2028, nobody needs a junior tester, and I only get about three more years before robots take the physical jobs too, so I can't just retrain as an electrician.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to my MP's surgery and join every campaign for public support, like a guaranteed income. I'd save every spare pound and move back to my parents' house in Long Eaton to halve my costs. I'd also ask my dad if the bus depot union has anything to say, because they'll be hit too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, to be honest. It feels like the ground has gone and everybody is still pretending to be normal. I'd lie awake doing sums on the loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame for this arriving so fast?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The companies racing each other, and the people who've let them do it with no rules. It's not the technology that makes me angry. It's that a few billionaires get to decide the pace for everyone, and people like me are told to 'adapt'.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your dad that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my dad I might lose the job within a year, and I'm sorry I took so long to get started. He'd say don't be daft, you've done nothing wrong, come home. That'd be the hardest and the kindest conversation.

say: Two years is **nothing**, and governments must act now.
I'd back anything that **slows it down** and supports people.
think: My computer science degree may be **worth little** before my career starts.
Robots follow about three years later, so I can't just **retrain** for hands-on work.
do: Go to my **MP's surgery** and back a guaranteed income.
Move back to my parents' house to **halve costs**.
Save every spare pound towards a cushion.
feel: **Scared**, as if the ground has gone while everyone pretends it's normal.
S2.quote: I'd tell my dad I might lose the job within a year, and I'm sorry I took so long to get started.
fieldNote: Fear is **political** as well as personal: he blames companies racing, not the technology.
Retreat to his parents' house is his real plan, and he finds it shaming.
Sees that robots only delay the hands-on trades by about three years.

steps.text: Write to my MP and attend a surgery about income support
Move back to my parents' house in Long Eaton
Save every spare pound in a cash account
Ask my dad to help with the loan if pay stops

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is long enough to do something, but it's also exactly long enough for people to put it off. I'd say at work that we need a proper plan now, not a panic in year four. Online I'd push for rules and a public fund that covers people who lose out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be slightly less frightened than with two years, because I'd be 27 by 2031 and could have paid some of the loan. But I'd still be competing against something that works for free. I'd have maybe three solid years in my job, and what I do next is the issue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the job and build one skill that isn't screen work. There's an evening course in electrical installation at Derby college, and I'd start it in January even though it's slow. I'd pay down the loan faster, because debt is the worst thing to have if my wages stop. And I'd stay in the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but not paralysed. I'd have a direction. I'd also feel annoyed that I'm the one adjusting, when the people who made the thing aren't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why electrical installation of all things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because by 2034 robots can do hands-on work as well as people, but installing in old terraced houses is awkward and every house is different. I'd guess that holds out longer. I'm not sure, and I know it only buys time, but it's better than waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course is a waste?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then it's a waste of about twelve hundred pounds and some tired Tuesday nights. That's a price I'd pay for having a plan. The thing I can't afford is doing nothing and being surprised.

say: We need a **proper plan** now, not a panic in year four.
I'd push for a **public fund** for people who lose out.
think: Five years gives me a little room to pay down **some of the loan**.
I'd still compete with something that works **for free**.
do: Start an **electrical installation** evening course at the Derby college in January.
feel: **Anxious** but not frozen, and annoyed that I'm the one adjusting.
S3.quote: The thing I can't afford is doing nothing and being surprised.
fieldNote: First scenario where he acts on his own **career** rather than politics.
His reasoning about hands-on work being awkward in old houses is plausible and honest about its limits.
Anger is aimed at the builders of the technology.

steps.text: Enrol on the evening electrical installation course at Derby college
Put an extra 150 pounds a month towards the student loan
Go to the union branch meetings every month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years feels almost like a normal career. I'd say at work that this is a long runway and we should use it well. Online I'd argue the timing is a chance to get rules, retraining funds and a shorter working week sorted properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel okay, maybe even a little hopeful. I'd be 32 in 2036, and with ten years I could change direction, pay off the loan and maybe buy a small house. My worry is that people will just use the long timeline to do nothing, and then be shocked in 2035.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on testing for now and keep learning the slow way. I'd take an apprenticeship-style route into something with real people in it, perhaps working with the council on transport software, because my dad's bus depot would use that. I'd also finally try the AI tools, one at a time, since by then they'd be part of any job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty steady, honestly. A bit more patient than I am now. I wouldn't feel safe, but I'd feel like I had a chance to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What stops people using the ten years well?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Habit. Everyone thinks it's someone else's job: government, the firm, the college. I'd say most of my friends would do nothing until year eight. My dad would still be driving buses in 2036, and he'd still believe it'll be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd try AI tools. Is that a change from now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and I notice it. Now I resist them because they feel like a threat. With ten years, I'd want to understand the thing that's changing my life, and a person who knows how it works has a better say than one who stays away.

say: Ten years is a **long runway**, so let's use it well.
I'd push for **retraining funds** and a shorter working week.
think: With a decade I could change direction and **pay off the loan**.
People may waste the time and be **shocked** in 2035.
do: Keep testing and **learn slowly** on the job.
Look for a role in **transport software** with the council.
Try AI tools one at a time.
feel: **Steady** and a little hopeful, with a chance to prepare.
S4.quote: A person who knows how it works has a better say than one who stays away.
fieldNote: Notable **softening**: ten years turns his resistance to AI into curiosity.
Pessimism about other people's habit of waiting, including his own father.
Still not calm; says he would not feel safe.

steps.text: Keep working as a tester while learning the product in depth
Apply to council transport software teams within three years
Try one AI testing tool a month and write notes

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most, because nobody has the time to get anything in place. What would help is a real income floor, a union that has a seat at the table, and a way to learn something useful without going into more debt. I'd also like my firm to promise in writing what happens to junior staff.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not against technology. I'm against people like me being told to cope on our own. If someone offered a fair deal, I'd happily learn any new tool. I just want a say.

headlineQuote: I'm not against technology. I'm against people like me being told to cope on our own.
portrait: Zane Ziegler is **22**, a junior software tester in Derby, a year out of a Nottingham computer science degree.
He rents a room in a shared house, owes about **eleven thousand** in student loan and keeps two months of rent saved.
He's progressive, backs unions and regulation, and resists new technology, so he **never uses AI tools** at first.
He moves from relief in mild worlds to **fear** at AGI in two years, then politics and moving home.
With ten years he softens, and says he would learn the tools to have a **fair say**.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because there would be **no time** for rules, retraining or a plan.
whatWouldHelp: A guaranteed **income floor**, a union seat at the table and retraining that doesn't add debt.
